title: Cambridge IELTS 20 Academic Listening Test 1 Part 3
description: Thảo luận học thuật giữa giáo sư và sinh viên chuẩn đề thi Cambridge IELTS 20 Test 1 Part 3.

lines.speaker: Speaker 1 (1)
lines.text: Part three.

lines.speaker: Speaker 1 (2)
lines.text: You will hear two sociology students called Tamara and Dev discussing their research for a presentation on loneliness.

lines.speaker: Speaker 1 (3)
lines.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26.

lines.speaker: Speaker 1 (4)
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (5)
lines.text: Shall we go through the notes we've made from our research into loneliness now, Dev?

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (6)
lines.text: Okay, Tamara.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (7)
lines.text: It's been a real eye opener.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (8)
lines.text: I had no idea that loneliness has been increasing steadily for the last twenty years.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (9)
lines.text: I know.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (10)
lines.text: And it's the same all over the world.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (11)
lines.text: The downside of a modern lifestyle, I guess.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (12)
lines.text: Did you come to any conclusions about what the reasons for the increase are?

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (13)
lines.text: Well, I'd assumed it was mainly an issue for the elderly, but in fact it's something which affects young people just as much.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (14)
lines.text: So nothing really to do with longer lifespans.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (15)
lines.text: Um, what about social media?

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (16)
lines.text: In my case, far from making me feel isolated, it actually does the opposite.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (17)
lines.text: It definitely does more good than harm.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (18)
lines.text: I say loneliness has a lot to do with the way cities are designed.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (19)
lines.text: People living in high rise flats with not much opportunity to speak to their neighbours.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (20)
lines.text: I think you're right.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (21)
lines.text: Another possible reason is that people are having fewer children and don't live in large extended family groups.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (22)
lines.text: But in this country anyway, that all changed decades ago and yet loneliness is a more recent problem.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (23)
lines.text: I suppose so.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (24)
lines.text: A more plausible explanation is that people are having to move around for work and often end up living miles away from their family and friends.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (25)
lines.text: That's true.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (26)
lines.text: Looking at the studies on health risks and loneliness, there are claims that loneliness has as much impact as smoking 15 cigarettes a day.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (27)
lines.text: Or similar to the risks caused by obesity.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (28)
lines.text: But I'm not sure there's enough evidence for some of these claims.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (29)
lines.text: Well, what about that one in Finland which showed that loneliness increased the risk of cancer by about ten percent.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (30)
lines.text: And those findings have been supported by other studies too.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (31)
lines.text: You're right about that one.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (32)
lines.text: I was actually thinking of the studies on dementia.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (33)
lines.text: Some found no association between loneliness and dementia and others found the opposite.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (34)
lines.text: Not exactly reliable then.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (35)
lines.text: There's been a lot of research on cardiovascular disease and whether loneliness contributes to that.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (36)
lines.text: Yes, I read that it was hard to reach a judgement as the definition of loneliness varied quite a lot and the responses from participants were too subjective.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (37)
lines.text: But there's no doubt that loneliness contributes to a weakened immune system.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (38)
lines.text: Unquestionably.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (39)
lines.text: The data on that is sound.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (40)
lines.text: What did you think about the evolutionary theory of loneliness?

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (41)
lines.text: Well, I thought the idea that loneliness evolved because it motivated people to be with other people quite convincing.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (42)
lines.text: Survival often depended on group cooperation.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (43)
lines.text: But I don't think there's enough evidence to claim that there must be a group of neurons in our brains which influence social behaviour by making us feel bad when we're alone.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (44)
lines.text: There are a few studies which support the theory, but not conclusively enough.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (45)
lines.text: More evidence is needed.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (46)
lines.text: And anyway, this theory's not really useful when it comes to solving the problem of loneliness today.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (47)
lines.text: True.

lines.speaker: Speaker 1 (48)
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.

lines.speaker: Speaker 1 (49)
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (50)
lines.text: Should we look at the relationship between loneliness and mental health now?

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (51)
lines.text: Okay.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (52)
lines.text: So loneliness and depression are clearly related and that's been recognised by various governments around the world.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (53)
lines.text: But unlike depression, loneliness has no recognised clinical form.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (54)
lines.text: There's no available diagnosis or effective treatments and that's not likely to change.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (55)
lines.text: I don't think so either.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (56)
lines.text: I was thinking we should start our presentation with an example from our own experience.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (57)
lines.text: I'd like to talk about how lonely I was when I started university, being away from home for the first time and all that.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (58)
lines.text: Good idea.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (59)
lines.text: Everyone will be able to relate to that, although a lot of students were probably too embarrassed to admit to it.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (60)
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (61)
lines.text: We could discuss ways of dealing with loneliness as well, like just talking to strangers.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (62)
lines.text: Loads of studies have shown that interactions with shop assistants and bar staff make people feel more optimistic and relaxed.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (63)
lines.text: I don't know about that, but it must make people feel more connected with their community.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (64)
lines.text: True.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (65)
lines.text: Although you need to be a certain kind of person to be able to just strike up a conversation.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (66)
lines.text: Good point.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (67)
lines.text: We should say something about solitude and how being alone and being lonely aren't the same thing.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (68)
lines.text: It's strange the way some people can't stand being by themselves while others love it.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (69)
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (70)
lines.text: The research shows a certain amount of solitude is beneficial for well-being, which I appreciate.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (71)
lines.text: But being alone isn't something I actually like.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (72)
lines.text: I'd never choose to go on holiday alone, for example.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2 (73)
lines.text: Me neither.

lines.speaker: Speaker 3 (74)
lines.text: Well, let's not

lines.speaker: Speaker 1 (75)
lines.text: That is the end of part three.

lines.speaker: Speaker 1 (76)
lines.text: You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to part three.
